sections.history: Thiruketheeswaram stands at Mathottam, the Mantai of old, once a busy harbour on the north-western coast of Sri Lanka facing Mannar island. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and one of only two in Eezha Nadu, the island's share of the Tevaram, the other being Koneswaram at Trincomalee. Thirugnana Sambandar and Sundarar both sang the Lord of Ketheeswaram, and Sundarar's verses dwell on the banks of the Palavi. The old shrine was destroyed in the late sixteenth century and worship there ceased for some three hundred years. In 1872 the Jaffna scholar Arumuka Navalar called on Shaivas to restore it; the site was traced in the 1890s and a new temple rose on the ancient ground in the early twentieth century.
sections.architecture: The present temple is a Dravidian shrine of the modern revival, raised on the site of the ancient one, with its sanctum for Ketheeswarar, a separate shrine for the Goddess and an enclosing prakaram. Its great sacred water is the Palavi tank, an ancient reservoir restored from ruin, whose name the Tevaram itself preserves. Near the temple lies the estuary of the Aruvi Aru, the river that once made Mathottam a port.
sections.legends: The name is explained through Ketu, the shadow planet of the navagrahas: tradition holds that Ketu performed penance at this spot and was granted the vision of Shiva and the Goddess, so that the place became Thiru-Ketu-Ishwaram. Another tradition links Mathottam with the Ramayana, saying that Mandodari, queen of Ravana, came from this port, and that her father Mayan, the celestial architect, first raised a shrine to Shiva here.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the great night of Thiruketheeswaram, when pilgrims gather from across the island to keep vigil, and on the following morning bathe in the Palavi tank. The annual Mahotsavam closes with a theertham, the sacred bathing of the deity at the Palavi; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Thiruketheeswaram is a place of return: a shrine that was lost for centuries and restored by the devotion of the people who remembered it. Pilgrims bathe in the Palavi, worship Ketheeswarar and the Goddess, and recall that Sambandar and Sundarar sang this coast from across the sea, joining Mathottam to the Shaiva sacred geography of the Tamil land.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions, with extended hours on Maha Shivaratri and festival days. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — men often enter the inner shrine bare-chested, wearing a veshti; women in saree or other modest dress. Footwear is left outside.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially during rituals and festivals.
visit.gettingThere: The temple lies on the mainland about 10 km from Mannar town, near the causeway to Mannar island, in Sri Lanka's Northern Province. Mannar has a railway station and bus links to Vavuniya, Anuradhapura and Jaffna; Colombo's international airport is the main gateway, several hours away by road.
